_insn_remainder: The four cases of 9173 that do not match are two encodings that never start an instruction anywhere in the function map: E034 appears only as the low word of pea.l operands (capstone also misdecodes it - roxr.l #8 for what silicon runs as roxr.b d0,d4 - but no rox instruction exists at any boundary in the map, so no rule is wrong on a path that exists), and 0072 00F6 01A0 01A0 sits inside data at 0x276c. The harness executes every distinct encoding it finds, code or not; silicon obliged, the port's rules for junk stay unverified, and that is the right place to leave them.
_names: Readability, ratcheted. addressNamed is how many routines are still called fn_<address>, which says where a routine came from and nothing about what it does; namedParams is how many parameters are more than the register they arrived in. The bar in DELIVERY.md is addressNamed 0, with every name backed by recorded evidence rather than being merely plausible - a wrong name is worse than an address, and 0x9080 was confidently called creditCompare while it drains an unrelated ring buffer. Move these numbers whenever a session names something: the edit is the record that the work happened. romlab/distinguish.py prints, per routine, the evidence needed to name it. The thing it showed: a colliding name is a name for a region (touches the player structs), and what separates its members is one level finer - the d(An) displacement, i.e. which field. No player routine reaches the struct by absolute address, so the field offsets are the whole distinguishing fact. Name the structs first and the routines name themselves; the other way round recovers the same field map forty-two times. 2026-08-01: the jump-stub rule now runs INSIDE the wrapper fixed point instead of once before it. It had a silent hole - the wrapper loop skips every `hop` address, so a stub whose target only became nameable later (because the target was itself a wrapper) could never be revisited, and stayed an address for ever. The two rules feed each other: a stub named this round is a callee for next round's wrapper, and a wrapper named this round is a target for next round's stub. Running both to a joint fixed point gives 48 wrappers and 31 of 67 stubs, and moves addressNamed from 539 to 537. A small number for the change, and worth saying why: most of those names already existed from the single pass, and what the fixed point adds is only the ones that were previously unreachable. The value is that the rule no longer depends on the order the two passes happen to run in, which is the kind of thing that silently stops working when something else moves. AND WHY THERE IS NO RULE LEFT FOR THE REMAINING 536, measured rather than assumed, so nobody spends a session looking for one. Of the unnamed routines, 415 have NO CALLERS AT ALL - they are inner entries reached by jump tables, tail jumps and lea(pc) continuations - so every caller-based rule is out for 77% of them: only 35 have exactly one caller that is itself named, and 44 have one to three all named. Proximity does not substitute: 536 of 537 have some named routine starting below them, but the median distance is 302 bytes and the commonest 'host' is a tiny wrapper with 86 entries after it, so naming by nearest-start-below would manufacture exactly the plausible-but-unchecked names this file exists to prevent. And of the 163 that genuinely sit INSIDE another routine's extent, the enclosing routine is unnamed in every single case - so the hosts have to be named first and the inner entries follow, not the other way round. That is the shape of the remaining work: it is evidence, one routine at a time, and DELIVERY.md was right to call it a bigger, less bounded grind. The two rules that DID generalise - wrappers named after their one callee, stubs named after where they jump - are now run to a joint fixed point and have given what they have to give. A NAMING FAULT FOUND WHILE TRACING, 2026-08-01, and it is the kind this file says is worse than an address. fn_07dce takes its d4 as `player_`, a role-inferred name - and at line 119 of its body assigns `player = (0x3e1968) >>> 0` and at line 143 uses it as `ptr`. The register is reused as a pointer for most of the routine, so the name is right for the first fifty lines and misleading for the rest. A scan for the same shape - a role-named parameter later reassigned to a constant address in work RAM - finds 331 of them. That is 331 of 2,852 named parameters - about one in eight - and the sentence that first stood here called it 'not a lot', which was written before the count came back and is simply wrong. It is a real defect rather than a missing name, and this file's own standard is that a wrong name costs more than fn_XXXXX does. Two ways to fix it and the second is better: refuse to name a parameter whose register is reassigned to an unrelated constant, or name it for what it holds on entry and let the reassignment introduce a new local, which is what a decompiler ought to do anyway since the two values have nothing to do with each other. roles.py assigns these names. The examples are not obscure ones either: kickWatchdogWrapper, helperInitialisePlayerStructs, wipeBoardRegionStartLevel (twice, in two different parameters), currentPieceDraw, cursorMove, counterReset and counterStep all take a parameter whose register is later pointed somewhere else entirely. So `namedParams` at 2,852 is an overcount of how much naming is actually TRUSTWORTHY: one in eight of those names is right on entry and wrong by the end of the routine. Worth fixing before the count is used as evidence of readability, because the readability bar in DELIVERY.md is about source somebody would choose to edit, and a parameter called `player` that holds a pointer halfway down is worse for an editor than one called d4. AND THE FIX IS IN, AT A COST THAT SHOULD BE STATED PLAINLY. roles.py now refuses to give a role name to a register that the routine later points at a constant address, because such a register is not one thing for the length of the routine and a role name claims it is. Result: routines with a parameter that stops being what it is called went from 331 to ZERO - and namedParams fell from 2852 to 2314, a loss of 538. That is a worse ratio than the 331 suggests, because the check is broader than the measurement was: it drops any register reassigned to a constant, not only ones reassigned into work RAM, and the extra couple of hundred are the same defect at other addresses. THE TRADE, argued rather than assumed: this file's standard is that a wrong name costs more than fn_XXXXX, and DELIVERY.md's bar is source somebody would choose to edit. A parameter called `player` that holds a pointer halfway down actively misleads the person editing, where `d4` merely tells them nothing. So fewer names that are true beats more names that are true for part of a routine. THE FLOOR IS LOWERED DELIBERATELY, from 2852 to 2314, which is the one thing a ratchet is not supposed to allow - recorded here so it is a decision on the record rather than a number that quietly slipped. The better fix, not done: name the parameter for what it holds on ENTRY and let the reassignment introduce a fresh local, since the two values have nothing to do with each other. That recovers the names honestly and is what a decompiler ought to do anyway.

_writes: Writes the two dispatchers agree on before the first that differs, the minimum over all six input patterns. It is the whole recorded run at the default cap - 300,000 - on all six patterns. That is NOT identity, and calling it identity was wrong: the cap is the instrument's bound, not the game's. Raising it to 1,000,000 on `one player` (2026-07-31) puts the first differing work-RAM write at 582,338, at 0x3e3280, recompiled 0x504e against decompiled 0x4fb3, with 0x3e3274 also apart at 0x1d18 against 0x1d10 - counters, under counterStep, in the same 0x3E32xx block the original goal named. So the honest statement is: identical for the first 300,000 writes on every pattern, and diverging at 582,338 on the one pattern measured past that. It was 27,004 and then 39,666. Four faults in the lift accounted for the difference, and three were rules m68kts.py already had right and only decomp.py had dropped: bclr/bset/bchg set no flags at all, so a branch after a bit test read a stale one; absolute short addressing did not sign-extend, so $ffff.w came out 0x0000FFFF where the chip makes it 0xFFFFFFFF; and the shifts set neither N nor Z. The fourth was double bookkeeping, a routine running past the end of its own case range being ticked twice for one instruction. When the lift and the oracle disagree, diff the two emitters before theorising. Past the cap the runs still part - see _compose, which is the same seam - and WRITE_CAP raises it. A FOURTH RULE OF THE SAME KIND, found 2026-08-01 by the same method and worth recording even though it moved no number: and/andi/or/ori/eor/eori set NO FLAGS in decomp.py, while m68kts.py calls m.logicFlags(_r, bits) after every one of them. The 68000 logic group sets N and Z from the result and clears C and V, so a branch after `or.b #$10,d0` was reading whatever an earlier instruction had left. Fixed the same way as the shifts. Measured after: the first differing write stays at 23,999 and the banner still differs, so nothing on the exercised paths depended on it - but it is a real hole and the fourth instance of the same pattern, which is the point. Every one of the four was a rule the recompiler had and the lifter had dropped, and all four were found by diffing the two emitters rather than by reasoning about the game. That is now the first thing to try, not the last. The suite is green after it, with the caveat in _flaky: the run that reported one failure was the slow one and a clean re-run passed. AND A SCAN THAT LOOKED ALARMING AND IS NOT, recorded so nobody re-runs it and panics. Diffing the two emitters mechanically for 'sets flags in m68kts.py, does not in decomp.py' returns 27 instructions including add, move, cmp, tst and clr. That is a false alarm: decomp.py sets self.flags in only THREE places in total (the shifts, the bit instructions, and the logic group fixed today), and yet 1,160 of 1,161 routines verify against the oracle. The reason is the design - flags are mostly DERIVED AT BRANCH POINTS by blocks.py from the comparison's own operands, not carried from the instruction that set them. So the mechanical diff cannot distinguish a real hole from a flag the branching pass reconstructs. What the four real faults have in common is sharper than 'the lift drops flags': in each, the flag a branch needs depends on a value computed EARLIER and not present at the branch - the pre-modification bit for bclr/bset/bchg, the result of a shift, the result of a logic op - so blocks.py has nothing to reconstruct it from. THE REFINED QUESTION, and a better use of the next session than re-diffing: which other instructions produce a flag that a later branch consumes without the branch seeing the operands? Enumerate those and the class is closed rather than sampled. AND THE REFINED QUESTION, ANSWERED IN THE NEGATIVE, which is the useful outcome. The natural candidate for 'a flag a branch cannot reconstruct' is C and V after arithmetic: N and Z can be recovered by re-reading the destination at the branch, but a carry cannot. blocks.py already handles exactly that - it models carry for the adds and the shifts explicitly and says so in comments at lines 392, 427 and 598, and COND at line 31 carries the full unsigned and overflow set. So that hypothesis is wrong and the branching pass is more complete than the mechanical diff implied. Taken with the calibration above, the picture is: flags are derived at branch points, carry and overflow included, and the four faults found were the genuine residue - cases where the needed value is neither at the branch nor modelled by a special kind - rather than four samples from a large pool. That is a reason to believe the class is nearly closed rather than a reason to keep grepping, and it is worth knowing before someone spends a session looking for a fifth. THE REMAINING DIVERGENCE, IN VALUES RATHER THAN COUNTS, which is the most concrete this has been. At write 23,999 of 25,655 on attract, windowed on 0x3E3200-0x3E32C0: 0x3e3280 takes 0x504e in the recompiled run and 0x4fb3 in the decompiled, and 0x3e3274 takes 0x1d18 against 0x1d10 - a difference of exactly 8. The writes are 16-bit pushes made by extractsOwnerBitsCellByte under counterStep. Two things follow. First, 0x4fb3 is ODD, so these are not return addresses being spilled - a 68000 return address is always even - which rules out the reading that this is the exception-frame seam wearing a different hat, and it is the reading that would otherwise be assumed given every other divergence in this file. Second, 0x1d18 against 0x1d10 differing by 8 looks like a counter or an index rather than a corrupted word, and counterStep is on the stack. So the shape is: something counted 8 further in one run than the other, and the value spilled downstream of it differs by a correspondingly small amount. NEXT: read extractsOwnerBitsCellByte and counterStep, and find what advances by 8 - a table stride, a per-entity step, or an iteration that ran once more. That is a question about two named routines with a measured symptom, which is a different kind of question from anything else left open here. AND counterStep IS A BCD COUNTER, which makes the difference of 8 mean something specific. The routine at 0x00E0E compares against 0x1e and 0x2 and carries setXAdd(t9, t10, 8) through every tick - the X flag from an 8-bit add, which is abcd/addx decimal arithmetic rather than binary. Read that way the divergent value fits exactly: 0x1d18 against 0x1d10 is a BCD low pair of 18 against 10, a decimal counter eight ahead in one run, not a corrupted word. And X is the flag with a known history here - it outlives the next instruction, it needed its own pass to carry through the lifted world (task #10), and it is the one flag the branching pass cannot rebuild at a branch because by definition it was set earlier. That is the same signature as the four faults already fixed. SO THE SUSPECT IS NAMED: X into or out of the decimal ops in counterStep and extractsOwnerBitsCellByte. Compare decomp.py and m68kts.py on abcd, sbcd, nbcd, addx, subx and negx specifically - the diff of the two emitters is how all four earlier faults were found, and this is the first lead that points at a group not yet diffed. UNPROVEN: the BCD reading of 0x1d18 is inference from the routine's constants, not a measurement. Confirm it by checking whether the value only ever holds digits 0-9 per nibble before spending time on the emitters. A FIFTH FAULT, FOUND AND NOT YET FIXED, with the fix specified. First correct the paragraph above: the BCD reading was WRONG. Neither emitter implements abcd/sbcd/nbcd (m68kts.py carries cycle costs for them but no emit rule), so the ROM does not use decimal arithmetic; setXAdd(t9, t10, 8) in counterStep is a plain add.b setting X, and 0x1e is thirty frames rather than a BCD bound. The counter is binary and differs by 8 outright. Now the fault. m68kts.py emits addx as m.addFlags(dst, src + (m.x ? 1 : 0), bits) - which sets the flags INCLUDING X. decomp.py writes ((dst) + (src) + extend()) and sets neither self.flags nor self.xstate. blocks.py emits setXAdd/setXSub from self.xstate, so with xstate unset after an addx the X flag is never updated: a multi-word add carries a STALE X into its next word, and X is precisely the flag the branching pass cannot rebuild because it was set earlier. That is the signature of all four faults already fixed. THE FIX: in decomp.py's addx/subx branch, set self.xstate to ('add', cur, '((src) + extend())', bits) for addx and the 'sub' kind for subx, so blocks.py emits the setX call. Not applied here - it needs the xstate tuple shape confirmed against blocks.py and a full regeneration to validate, and applying it unverified at the end of a session is how the earlier wrong turns happened. Note addx's Z is also unusual (cleared if the result is non-zero, otherwise left alone) so do not set self.flags with the ordinary cmp shape without checking that. AND THE FIFTH FAULT DOES NOT SURVIVE EITHER - withdrawn before anyone acts on it. decomp.py has no xstate at all; that mechanism belongs to blocks.py, and the two are separate classes, so 'decomp.py fails to set xstate' was never the right test. blocks.py DOES handle addx and subx: it calls self.sync_flags() at line 400 so that extend() reads the X the chip would have, and it carries a comment naming this ROM's idiom - `add.b d6,d6` followed by `addx.w d0,d0`, repeated, which reads X five times to shift five bytes' top bits into one word. Each add sets X through the addends path; each addx consumes it. So addx never needs to SET X for the code this ROM actually contains, and the author had already reasoned about precisely this case. Two lessons, both cheap to state and expensive to relearn. First, the mechanical emitter diff that found four real faults ALSO produced three false ones in a row here (27 flag rules, C/V after arithmetic, addx's X) - it is a lead generator, not an oracle, and each hit needs the branching pass checked before it counts. Second, when this file already carries a comment about the exact instruction pair in question, read it first: it was written by someone who had the measurement in front of them. A QUALIFICATION ON THIS ENTRY'S OWN HEADLINE, which reads stronger than the measurement supports. 'Every write to work RAM matches - 300,000, the cap - so this is no longer a floor but an assertion of identity' is true only UP TO THE CAP. 300,000 is where the harness stops recording, not where the runs part. The narrow window on 0x3E3200-0x3E32C0 diverges at its own write 23,999, and because that window catches only a sliver of traffic, its 23,999th write happens far later in absolute time than the broad window's 300,000th. The two results are therefore consistent and the broad one simply stops before reaching the divergence - it is a floor after all, wearing the language of an identity claim. What would settle the real first divergence in work RAM is the broad window with a raised cap, and _writes already records that WRITE_CAP=3,000,000 kills the vitest worker (five Int32Arrays that size), so the usable move is an intermediate cap around 1,000,000, or recording only the first difference rather than every write. Worth doing early next session: every claim in this file about where the runs first differ rests on which window and which cap was in force, and that has not been stated alongside the numbers until now. AND THE MEASUREMENT WAS RUN: WRITE_CAP=1000000 on the full 0x3E0000-0x400000 window, attract, 400 frames. The first divergence in ALL of work RAM is write 576,838 - so the two dispatchers agree on 576,837 consecutive writes, nearly twice the cap that was being reported as identity. And it is the SAME divergence the narrow window found: 0x3e3280 taking 0x504e against 0x4fb3 and 0x3e3274 taking 0x1d18 against 0x1d10, pushed by extractsOwnerBitsCellByte under counterStep. Two things follow. The narrow window was finding the genuine first divergence rather than a local artefact, which retrospectively validates every measurement made through it tonight. And the real number is 576,837, not 300,000 - the shipped default cap is 300,000 so the floor cannot simply be raised to it without raising the cap too, and raising the cap costs memory (WRITE_CAP=3,000,000 kills the worker). The honest options are: raise both to 600,000 and keep the identity claim true to the divergence, or leave the cap and stop calling 300,000 an assertion of identity. The second is free and the first is better; either is more accurate than what is there now. AND IT IS NOW WHAT IT CLAIMS TO BE. The cap is raised to 600,000 and the floor to 576,837, the measured first divergence, and the harness passes at that setting on every pattern - so the minimum across all six clears it. The number in this file is now the point at which the two dispatchers actually part rather than the point at which the harness stopped looking, which is the difference between an assertion and an artefact. 600,000 and not more because WRITE_CAP=3,000,000 kills the worker on five Int32Arrays of that size; 600,000 costs about 12MB and thirteen seconds. If a future fix pushes the divergence past 600,000 the cap has to move with it, and the failure mode is quiet - the run will report 'identical, 600,000' and the floor will pass while measuring nothing new - so raise both together or the same confusion returns. AND THE SHAPE OF THE REMAINING DIVERGENCE, which writes.test's own comment had already guessed. extractsOwnerBitsCellByte at 0x00FB4 reads load32(dst + -0x12) three times - that is -$12(a6), the frame local the comment beside run.a6 names - along with -0xd, -0xc, -0x8 and -0x4, and pushes the results. a6 is IDENTICAL in both runs at 0x3e3286, and by that comment's own rule (same a6 with different contents means residue, different a6 means the caller) this is RESIDUE: the routine reads a frame local it never initialised, holding whatever the stack last left there. That would explain everything observed - the value differs without any instruction being mis-lifted, which is why every routine in the chain passes the oracle on random states; it is stable once it happens, because the residue does not change; and it is ultimately traceable to the seam, since what the two runs last left on the stack differs by exactly the exception frames pushed at different points, which is the one difference this file has documented from the start. If that is right the remaining divergence is not a lifting fault at all but the game reading uninitialised stack, and the two dispatchers can only agree there if their stack residue agrees. UNPROVEN: read the routine's prologue and confirm nothing writes -$12(a6) before the first read, then dump that word in both runs a few instructions earlier. If confirmed, say so plainly in this file - it changes what 'agree through an entire game' can mean. HALF-CONFIRMED, and the other half moves it up a level - so do not bank the residue story yet. Confirmed: nothing in extractsOwnerBitsCellByte stores to -0x12 before the first load32(dst + -0x12), so the routine does not initialise it. Not confirmed: the routine takes `dst` as a PARAMETER (dst = dst_) rather than establishing a frame with link, so a6 is inherited and -$12(a6) is a local of the CALLER's frame, not of this one. A caller that wrote it would make the value ordinary data rather than residue, and then the question is simply why the caller's data differs - which is the same question one level up, not an answer. THE NEXT STEP IS THEREFORE SPECIFIC: check counterStep, and whatever calls it, for a store to -0x12(a6) before the call. If one exists, follow that value; if none does anywhere up the chain until a link, the residue reading stands and with it the conclusion that the game reads uninitialised stack. This is the fourth time tonight that a clean-looking conclusion needed one more check before it held, and each time the check was cheaper than the correction would have been. AND THE CALL CHAIN PUTS IT INSIDE THE INTERRUPT HANDLER, which reopens the seam explanation this entry closed a few paragraphs ago. The ROM stack at the divergence is identical in both runs - 0x10000 <- 0xdda <- 0x135d6 <- 0x132b6 <- 0x11efe <- 0x137b0 <- 0xdfe <- 0xee7e <- 0x9202 - and 0x135d6 and 0x132b6 sit beside 0x133b2, the frame interrupt handler this file names throughout. So the divergent write happens INSIDE the handler, and the a6 frame that -$12(a6) belongs to is built on top of the exception frame - the one structure documented from the beginning as differing between the two dispatchers, in the stacked program counter and the condition codes, because the chip interrupts between instructions and the lifted code at a block head. Neither extractsOwnerBitsCellByte nor counterStep writes -0x12 or establishes a frame with link; a6 is inherited by both, so the owner is further up this chain and inside the handler. THE TENSION TO RESOLVE, stated plainly because it is the crux: an earlier paragraph here ruled out the exception frame on the grounds that 0x4fb3 is odd and a stacked PC is always even. That argument still holds for the VALUE being a program counter, but not for the value being DERIVED from a frame whose contents differ - a word combined with condition codes, or a local overlapping the frame, would be odd quite legitimately. So the exception frame is back as the leading explanation and the odd -address argument only narrows what the value can be, not where it came from. NEXT: identify which routine in that chain establishes the frame, and dump the words around a6 in both runs at that point. AND THE TWO READINGS COLLAPSE INTO ONE, which is where this ends tonight. Not one routine in the chain establishes a frame - counterStep, powerSelfTestFrom3, decompressOneEightPixelColumn and ramTestAllPatternsFrom3 all inherit a6 and none stores -0x12. And a6 is 0x3e3286, which is not a pointer into a data structure at all: it is in the STACK, the same region as the writes. So -$12(a6) is 0x3e3274 - one of the two divergent addresses exactly - and the routine is reading stack scratch below an inherited frame pointer. That is residue, and it is residue in precisely the region where the two dispatchers push their exception frames, which differ by design in the stacked program counter and condition codes. So the residue reading and the seam reading were never alternatives: the residue IS the seam, observed through a routine that reads below its own frame. Everything fits - no instruction is mis-lifted, so every routine passes the oracle; the value is stable once it happens, because the residue does not change; it appears inside the interrupt handler, because that is what pushed the frame; and the odd value 0x4fb3 is fine, because stack scratch is not a program counter. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE GOAL, stated because it is a bound rather than a bug: the two dispatchers can agree here only if their stack residue agrees, and their exception frames differ by design. Byte-identity through a whole game therefore requires either making the frames identical - which the interruptFrame note explains is not available - or accepting that reads of uninitialised stack are outside the comparison, the way interruptFrame is already excluded. UNPROVEN in one respect: that the game's behaviour actually depends on this value rather than discarding it. Check that before concluding the game is affected at all. AND EVIDENCE ON WHETHER IT MATTERS, already in hand and worth connecting to the paragraph above rather than leaving in _screens. The frame sweep found the two runs' visible screens IDENTICAL at 600 frames after differing at 400 and 500 - a full reconvergence. That is evidence the residue is largely discarded: a value the game depended on durably could not let the picture come back into agreement. But the banner differs at 700, so something does survive somewhere. The two facts together suggest the residue is consumed by most readers and retained by at least one, which is a narrower claim than either 'it is benign' or 'it is a real fault' and is as far as the measurements reach. HOW TO SETTLE IT, and it is cheap: the residue at 0x3e3274 is read by extractsOwnerBitsCellByte and pushed. Force that word to a fixed value in both runs - a one-line poke in the harness, not a change to the port - and re-run the frame sweep. If the banner then agrees at 700, the residue is the whole cause and the bound in the paragraph above is the real answer. If the banner still differs, there is a second cause and the residue is a red herring for the visible fault, however well it explains the write. That experiment distinguishes the two remaining stories in a single run, and it is the first thing to do next. CORROBORATION ALREADY IN THE PATTERN LIST, which is cheaper than the poke experiment and points the same way. _compose records that `service switch` is the ONE pattern of six that never diverges, and that 0x130B0, the self-test driver, raises the interrupt mask to level 7 for its whole duration so no frame interrupt arrives while it runs. No interrupts means no exception frames pushed into the stack region, which means no differing residue at 0x3e3274 - exactly what the residue story predicts, on a pattern nobody chose for this purpose. That was already noted as evidence for 'the divergence is the seam' before the mechanism was known; with the mechanism it is sharper, because the seam and the residue are now the same object rather than two things that happen to correlate. It does not remove the need for the poke experiment - that one distinguishes whether the residue causes the VISIBLE banner fault, which is a different question from whether it causes the write - but it does mean the write-level story now has two independent lines of evidence and no measurement against it. AND THE TRUE ORIGIN, WHICH THE INSTRUMENT WAS HIDING BY DESIGN. writes.test returns early on any write made while an exception frame is being pushed - `if (sys.m.inFrame && !FRAME_BYTES) return;` at line 139 - so every number this entry reports is downstream of the frame pushes rather than inclusive of them. Run with FRAME_BYTES=1 and the first difference is at write 12,629, not 576,838: FORTY-FIVE TIMES EARLIER. The differing write is 0x3e32bc taking 0x4516 in the recompiled run and 0x4510 in the decompiled - both even, both in ROM range, so these are STACKED PROGRAM COUNTERS six bytes apart, which is precisely the six bytes CLAUDE.md describes for a frame pushed at a different instant. The stack names the site: takeIrq under soundChannelDispatch under soundSequencePlayer, the sound driver's busy-wait, the loop this project has known from the start leaves at different iterations in the two runs. So the whole chain is now one story with one origin: the two dispatchers leave the sound wait at different points, push frames whose stacked PC differs by six, that difference sits in the stack as residue, a routine reads it at -$12(a6) as uninitialised scratch, and it reaches the screen as a green station banner. THE QUALIFICATION THIS FORCES: '576,837 writes identical' means identical EXCLUDING exception frames. That is a defensible thing to measure - the frames differ by design and interruptFrame exists to mark them - but it is not what the words say, and the honest statement is 'identical apart from the frames themselves, which differ from write 12,629'. Both numbers should be reported together from now on. CORRECTION TO THE PARAGRAPH ABOVE, made immediately and before it is built on: 0x4516 and 0x4510 are NOT stacked program counters. There is no code at 0x4510-0x451F anywhere in the decompiled source - the string '0x0451' does not occur - and neither address is among the 8,210 members of POLL_AT, so they cannot be a program counter the lifted world would ever stack. 'Even and in ROM range' was the whole basis for that reading and it was not enough. The 38-cycle difference reported before was entirely the artefact suspected, and this confirms it by measurement rather than by argument. So the schedule is not drifting, the deadlines are not drifting, and the six candidate causes eliminated so far are: cost accounting, the interrupt service point, the handoff discount as a global change, the SR mask, `next` drift, and now the frame schedule itself. What that leaves is subtle and worth stating exactly: the sampler reads sys.frames BEFORE System.run increments it, so a poll at which one side crosses reports the old count. Frames 133/134 at the same index is therefore consistent with both sides crossing at the same CYCLE but at ADJACENT POLLS - which is possible because the poll points themselves are not at identical cycle counts even when the clocks agree at the sampled ones. The remaining question is no longer 'why do they cross at different times' - they do not - but 'why does one side have a poll between the crossing and the other side's next poll'. That is a question about POLL_AT membership, not about timing.
